He identifies as Mexican American and Filipino American and is comfortable saying that both descriptions matter to him.
His mother’s side of the family has strong Mexican American roots, while his father’s family has Filipino American roots and its own stories of migration and work.
English is his everyday language, though he recognizes Spanish phrases and family expressions from years of hearing relatives speak.
He is not religiously affiliated and does not attend services as a regular practice.
He sometimes joins family observances and holiday meals because the relationships and memories matter to him, even when he does not share religious belief.
He completed an occupational certificate at community college before later completing his bachelor's degree through a transfer and online-completion route.
His bachelor's degree did not lead to a high-paying career, and he does not regard that fact as proof that education was pointless.
He learned much of his most useful work knowledge from experienced maintenance workers who showed him how to diagnose a problem without wasting materials.
He has an old tool bag from his maintenance years that he keeps even though he no longer takes on demanding repair jobs.
His apartment is modest but arranged around familiarity: a comfortable chair, a small television, his phone charger, and photographs he does not want to pack away.
He has a rent subsidy that makes his apartment more stable than it would otherwise be on disability income.
He occasionally receives groceries or a ride from family, but would rather ask for a specific favor than make a general appeal for help.
His financial situation is worse than it was four years ago, largely because of the loss of his wife's income and the lasting effects of her illness and his own work limitations.
He nevertheless reports no inflation-related hardship in the specific sense that rising prices have not forced him to skip a bill or essential purchase.
He can say that the national economy is excellent while also saying that his own household has become poorer; he does not experience those statements as contradictory.
He does not spend much time reading books, but will read a benefit notice several times if he is worried that misunderstanding it could affect his housing or income.
He is more likely to learn from a short video or a demonstration than from a long written guide.
He has no particular interest in cooking, although he can make a few reliable meals and enjoys food prepared by relatives.
He has no particular interest in pets and does not currently live with an animal.
He has no particular interest in gaming, crafts, board games, or shopping as recreation.
He has no particular interest in travel and is content to stay close to home most of the time.
His neighborhood walks are functional and familiar; he does not describe himself as an outdoorsman.
He often checks social media before he has fully woken up and later wishes he had waited until after breakfast.
A familiar television episode can be comforting because he does not have to concentrate hard or decide what to watch.
He dislikes being told that he should simply be more positive about grief, disability, or money.
He appreciates help that is specific, such as a ride at a particular time or someone sitting with him while he completes a form.
He can be skeptical of a new device or product while still being genuinely curious about the larger idea it represents.
He is more comfortable with an established routine than with a sudden change, especially when the change affects money, sleep, or medical care.
He does not see his conservative views as incompatible with supporting selected background-check measures and mental-health funding.
He believes there is a meaningful difference between supporting a policy and assuming that it will solve a problem by itself.
He has become less willing to argue about politics with relatives whose relationships matter more to him than winning a conversation.
He worries about political violence and feels that public figures should speak more carefully about opponents and elections.
He is not very confident that elections are fair, but does not claim to possess hidden proof that a particular election was fraudulent.
He disapproves of the Supreme Court and worries that public trust is being damaged by partisan conflict.
He is strongly opposed to abortion in most cases but understands that people facing a difficult pregnancy may have circumstances he cannot see from the outside.
He supports a path to legal status for some undocumented immigrants while wanting immigration rules to be clearer and enforceable.
He is concerned about drug addiction because he has seen its effects on people and families, not just because it is a campaign talking point.
He considers healthcare affordability a major public problem even though he does not want government to run healthcare as a universal responsibility.
His strongest near-term measure of success is not a dramatic career change; it is having a stable place to live, manageable pain, and a few relationships he can count on.
